analysis.one_liner: Transfers the U.S. Postal Service to a private corporation whose stock goes first to employees, then to public investors.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee and two subcommittees in 1991 and never received a hearing vote or floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would hand all property of the U.S. Postal Service — its buildings, network, and legal rights — to a private corporation incorporated by up to nine people chosen in an employee election. For one year, the corporation's stock could only be issued to postal employees, with shares based on years of service and pay; after that, shares could be sold to the general public. The President would write a plan to abolish the Postal Service, and the legal monopoly on first-class mail would stay with the new private corporation for its first five years.
analysis.who_benefits: The new private corporation and its future shareholders, who would acquire a public asset — the entire postal network and its legal monopoly on mail delivery. Postal employees would receive stock, though shares would be weighted by pay level, so the highest-compensated managers would receive the most. Private investors could buy in after the first year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The new private corporation and shareholders

how_it_helps.text: The bill transfers all U.S. property and rights of the Postal Service to a private corporation, converting a public institution into private property [S3].
Corporate stock would first be issued only to postal employees, allocated by years of service and level of compensation, then could be sold to the general public after one year [S3].

The President would transmit a transfer plan to Congress including recommendations for abolishing the Postal Service, and the private express statutes — the laws giving the Post Office its monopoly on letter carriage — would continue with the corporation for its first five years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public, which owns the Postal Service as a civic asset built over two centuries. If it passed, Americans would see their postal network become a private company's property; the bill leaves rate-setting during the transition to proposals the President develops, and rural and high-cost delivery routes — which lose money but are required to be served under universal service rules — would depend on whatever the new corporation and the White House worked out.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public owning a shared civic asset

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself guarantee postal rates or universal service in the new corporation's hands; it only requires the corporation to include delivery consistent with existing universal-service and rate principles among its purposes, and leaves the actual rate-setting mechanism for the transition to presidential proposals developed after consulting the Postal Rate Commission [S3].

The corporation would be incorporated by no more than nine individuals elected by postal employees, with the President empowered to impose whatever additional requirements he chooses by regulation — concentrating control of a nationwide public network in a handful of incorporators and the executive branch [S3].

The legal monopoly on letter mail would remain with a private, shareholder-owned corporation for its first five years, so the public would get a private monopoly rather than either a public service or competition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers employees stock and the public shares of a company, but what it gives away is a public asset: the national mail network and its legal monopoly. The safeguards it includes — comparable retirement benefits and a required purpose of consistent universal service — are weaker than the current law's binding universal service obligation, and the actual rate and service rules for the transition would be written later by the President. An honest supporter of privatization would have to acknowledge that this version transfers control before any of the hard questions about rates, rural routes, and service guarantees are answered.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Post Office and Civil Service Committee, which farmed it out to two subcommittees in June 1991, and it sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing vote, no committee report, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on February 25, 1991, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service [S1] [S5].

On June 7, 1991, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Postal Personnel and Modernization and the Subcommittee on Postal Operations and Services, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted five Republican cosponsors and no committee action, and it expired with the 102nd Congress in January 1993 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's ownership of the postal system was untouched; no private corporation acquired the network or its monopoly, and postal employees kept their status as employees of a public service.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept its postal system public

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to privatize the Postal Service on February 25, 1991.

for.name: 5 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members of either party signed on.

against.name: House Post Office and Civil Service Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in February 1991, referred it to two subcommittees in June 1991, and never reported it out or scheduled any action on it.

against.name: Postal worker unions
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed privatization of the Postal Service, which would have ended their members' federal employment status and converted their agency into a shareholder-owned company.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, and the bill died in a committee controlled by Democrats without any vote, so no roll-call shows how the chamber as a whole would have split.

industries.industry: The new private postal corporation and its shareholders
industries.note: The corporation would acquire the entire public postal network and keep the legal monopoly on letter carriage for its first five years, converting a public service into a shareholder-owned company. Ordinary people would face a private monopoly on their mail rather than either a public service or competition.

Employees would receive company stock allocated by years of service and pay — meaning the best-paid managers would get the most — and comparable retirement benefits, but their employer would change from a public service to a private corporation whose jobs and routes could be restructured. Higher-paid managers gain the most from the stock formula.

industries.industry: Private mail and express carriers (UPS, FedEx and similar firms)
industries.note: The bill keeps the private express statutes in force for five years, so rivals could not immediately compete for letter mail; any opening of the market would come only through later presidential recommendations and congressional action.

industries.industry: Postal Rate Commission and the public rate-setting framework
industries.note: The Postal Rate Commission, which sets postage rates under public process, would be abolished as part of the transfer, with its future role left to presidential proposals during a five-year transition.
